newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 7.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--OTE, Greece's telecoms organisation, will maintain its monopoly in the Greek market until December 12, 2000, two years later than other EU countries. The official announcement on the extension of OTE's monopoly will be made within the month but the substance of the decision has been formalised in negotiations between Commissioner Karel Van Miert and Greek Transport and Communications Minister Haris Kastanidis. Most other EU countries will see deregulated telecoms systems as of January 1, 1998 while Greece's Cohesion Fund partners Ireland and Portugal will open their telecoms doors as of December 31, 1999.
--Moving Olympic Airways, Greece's national carrier, to the new international airport at Spata, will cost approximately 127 billion drachmas, according to initial estimates.
--The drachma fell against the basket of European currencies in the month of April in comparison to March, according to the latest figures from the Ionian Bank's department of financial studies.

--April inflation will be below 6.0 percent, public revenue collection is seeing a marked improvement and the state budget is being executed according to schedule, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou told Prime Minister Costas Simitis at their meeting yesterday.

--Following the International Monetary Fund's recommendation that the pace of privatisation be stepped up, the government is planning specific measures to open up the banking sector and major projects to private initiative and to contain the role of the state.
--Today will see the first meeting of a special committee formed to enable OTE to adjust to new deregulated market conditions as of 2001.

--State spending and delays in the merger of similar organisations in the wider (primarily banking) public sector were the first serious complaints heard from the International Monetary Fund delegation visiting Athens to evaluate the course of the economy. The rate of reducing state spending is extremely low, the IMF delegation said.

--The finance ministry is now planning its next moves on the interest rates front, with plans for the first rate cut in a month, following the news that April inflation has seen a further drop. The next issue of state securities will involve cpi indexed-bonds of five- and 10-year duration, sources say.

--The IMF delegation is reported to have reservations about whether the government will achieve budget targets, following talks with experts and officials at the State Audit Council. Sources say the delegation believes the targets are ambitious and the measures to meet them fall short.

--The development ministry is concerned about the negative climate which has been created in certain ailing companies, such as Softex and the Elefsis Shipyards. Worker unrest at the enterprises, Deputy Development Minister Anna Diamantopoulos said yesterday, may have irreversibly negative consequences on the continued operation of the firms, on jobs and on their privatisation.

--Ionian Bank will distribute one new share for each five held by stockholders, the administration decided yesterday. The 1996 balance sheet is expected to show a pre-tax profit of five billion drachmas but figures so far this year are more encouraging.

--Prime Minister Simitis will present awards to 15 businessmen and businesses for their efforts to increase business activity in Greece at today's Athens Chamber of Commerce and Industry annual ceremony. In his address, Simitis is expected to broach current issues of concern, such as growth, competitiveness and employment.
--There appears to be hope on the horizon for a resolution of differences that will see work get going again on the Athens Metro. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
